title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter
text:

[3]Because the lamp had to burn from dusk until dawn, someone always stayed awake.[/3] Ada often took the midnight watch herself.

In her diary, which our family still keeps, she describes the work with surprising affection. Trimming wicks, polishing brass, and [4]to log[/4] passing ships were chores she performed with pride. The isolation[5] she wrote,[/5] never felt lonely; the sea was "company enough." [6]Her father, was[/6] stern about one rule: the light came before everything, including sleep, meals, and even holidays.

[10]Today the lighthouse runs on automated LEDs.[/10] No keeper climbs the stairs, and no one trims a wick by lamplight. But when I visit Cape Warren, I like to think the light still carries a little of Ada's stubborn devotion.

title: The Science of Sourdough
text:
Every sourdough loaf begins with a starter: a bubbling paste of flour and water that [1]harbor[/1] wild yeast and bacteria. Bakers feed the mixture daily, and in return the microbes produce the carbon dioxide that makes bread [2]rise and the acids[/2] that give sourdough its distinctive tang.

[3]Bread has been baked for thousands of years.[/3] Lactic acid bacteria, the same family of organisms found in yogurt, compete and cooperate with yeast in a delicate balance. When the balance shifts—because of temperature, hydration, or the flour [4]itself—the[/4] flavor of the bread shifts with it.

A starter from Mexico City behaved differently [6]then[/6] one from Helsinki, even when both were fed identical flour. [7]Some starters have been passed down through families for more than a century, traveling across oceans in jars tucked into suitcases.[/7]

For home bakers, this variability is part of the appeal. [8]One cannot ever ascertain in advance the loaf's precise gustatory profile, which constitutes its appeal.[/8] A sourdough starter is less like a recipe [9]and more like a pet,[/9] it must be fed, watered, and occasionally forgiven. [10]Ultimately, the loaf on the counter is a record of every kitchen it has ever lived in.[/10]

title: Murals of the Mission District
text:

title: The Forgotten Builders
text:

Avalanches buried camps without warning. [4]Despite these conditions, the crews advanced with remarkable speed,[/4] at one point laying ten miles of track in a single day.

For decades, however, textbooks barely mentioned [6]them.[/6] Their wages were lower than those of other crews, and their names rarely appeared in company documents. [8]These objects are old.[/8] Descendants of the workers now gather each year at Promontory Summit, [9]where the rails once met, to honor[/9] their ancestors' labor. [10]The celebration grows larger every year.[/10] History, they argue, should finally show the hands that laid the track.

title: Summer at the Radio Station
text:

title: The Return of the Bison
text:

The transfers, which began as a small pilot program, now move hundreds of animals across state lines each autumn.

[5]Bison are large animals.[/5] Their hooves aerate compacted soil, their wallows collect rainwater for amphibians, and their grazing patterns [6]creates[/6] a patchwork of grasses that supports ground-nesting birds. [7]Prairie dogs also dig burrows.[/7]

[10]As the gate opened, the animals hesitated—then poured onto the prairie like water finding an old channel.[/10]

title: Jazz in the Archives
text:

Some recordings are so fragile that playing them once [3]destroy[/3] them forever; the archivists digitize these in a single, carefully planned pass.

[4]The work requires equal parts chemistry and patience.[/4] Old tape sheds its magnetic coating like autumn leaves, so technicians bake reels in a low oven to stabilize them. A cylinder from 1904 recently yielded a street vendor's song [5]that scholars had known only from, a newspaper description.[/5]

[7]Her improvisations were interesting.[/7] Musicians now study the recording; one composer based an entire suite [8]off of[/8] its final four minutes.

[9]Funding, of course, is never guaranteed, the archivists write grants between repair sessions.[/9] They argue that a city's sound is as much a landmark as its buildings. title: The Glassblower's Apprentice
text:

[5]The studio had several furnaces.[/5] When Marisol finally shaped a bubble with even walls, he said only, "Again." She made forty more that afternoon. [6]Later she understood, that[/6] repetition was the real curriculum; the vase was just a byproduct.

title: Mapping the Ocean Floor
text:

[3]Ships with multibeam sonar do the most precise work.[/3] The instrument sends fans of sound pulses toward the bottom, [4]it measures[/4] the echo's return time to calculate depth. But survey ships are slow and expensive, [5]consequently, an[/5] international project called Seabed 2030 is recruiting help: cargo vessels, fishing fleets, and even private sailboats now donate their depth readings.

The discoveries have been anything but dull. Mappers have found underwater volcanoes taller than the Alps, canyons that [6]dwarfs[/6] the Grand Canyon, and shipwrecks resting undisturbed for centuries. [7]In 2022, a survey near an Australian reef revealed a coral tower taller than the Empire State Building—healthy, teeming, and previously unknown.[/7]

[8]Why does any of this matter to people on land?[/8] Ocean currents, which regulate climate, follow the contours of the deep. [9]Fisheries depend on seamounts. title: The Community Garden Debate
text:

title: Typewriters and Their Devotees
text:

[9]Critics dismiss the trend as nostalgia, and maybe it is.[/9] But nostalgia has rarely been this productive. title: The Physics of Figure Skating
text:
A triple axel lasts less than a second, but inside that second [1]lies[/1] a small physics lecture. Angular momentum stays constant, so the spin [3]accelerates, this is[/3] the same principle that speeds a twirling ice dancer or a collapsing star. Jumping, [4]for example,[/4] is only half the problem. Landing multiplies the skater's weight [5]by five or six times[/5], all of it absorbed on a single blade about four millimeters wide. [7]The ice itself participates in the physics.[/7] Rink temperature changes the surface's hardness: figure skaters prefer [8]softer ice, hockey players like it harder and faster.[/8] Arena managers adjust the refrigeration accordingly, sometimes between events on the same day.

[9]Coaches increasingly use this research.[/9] Some now cap the number of jump repetitions in practice, [10]protecting young athletes' joints while they are still developing.[/10] The sport's artistry conceals its engineering—which may be exactly why audiences gasp.

title: Letters from the Homestead
text:

title: The Night Market
